subject: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992)
object: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992) described 2 sibs born to consanguineous parents who had a multiple congenital anomaly pattern. It included low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas and hypospadias.

subject: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992)
object: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992) concluded that the constellation of anomalies in sibs born to consanguineous parents appeared to represent a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome.

subject: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992)
object: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992) searched the data files of the Spanish Collaborative Study of Congenital Malformations (ECEMC). They found 3 other unrelated infants with intestinal atresias, hypospadias and low birth weight, and suggested these cases may represent a milder expression of the same syndrome.

subject: Annerén et al. (1998)
object: Annerén et al. (1998) described a lethal syndrome with intrauterine growth retardation, intra- and extrahepatic biliary atresia, and esophageal and duodenal atresia. They considered it to be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

subject: Gentile and Fiorente (1999)
object: Gentile and Fiorente (1999) reported a case with esophageal, duodenal, rectoanal and biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation, a malformed/hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. They considered this further evidence of a new distinct syndrome.

subject: Mitchell et al. (2004)
object: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants (2 sibling pairs from 2 families and 1 isolated case) with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. One sibling pair was born to consanguineous parents. Four children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management, and 1 patient with a milder form was surviving without insulin.

subject: Mitchell et al. (2004)
object: Mitchell et al. (2004) performed pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 of the infants. It showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin staining at all. Exocrine histology varied between cases.

subject: Mitchell et al. (2004)
object: Mitchell et al. (2004) concluded that the condition probably represents a new autosomal recessive syndrome. Their evidence was the affected sibling pairs, one of which was born to consanguineous parents.

subject: Mitchell et al. (2004)
object: In 1 patient from the consanguineous family, Mitchell et al. (2004) found no duplication or uniparental isodisomy of PLAGL1 at 6q24 and no contiguous gene deletion involving the glucokinase gene. They also found no mutation in the coding sequences or splice sites of PDX1.

subject: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007)
object: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007) described a female infant born to consanguineous parents who had a multiple congenital anomaly pattern of low birth weight, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas and intestinal malrotation. She died 60 days after birth. High-resolution chromosome analysis (550-600 bands) was normal (46,XX).

subject: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007)
object: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007) concluded that their patient, born to consanguineous parents, confirmed the autosomal recessive disorder previously described by their group (Martínez-Frías syndrome).

subject: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007)
object: Galán-Gómez et al. (2007) suggested that the pathogenesis of the syndrome is most probably of blastogenetic origin, mainly affecting the midline developmental duodenal-biliary-pancreatic junction.

subject: Chappell et al. (2008)
object: Chappell et al. (2008) reported a patient born to consanguineous parents who had neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis. This was the first such case with neonatal diabetes and no demonstrable structural abnormality of the pancreas, which the authors said showed that a deficit in pancreatic function is involved.

subject: Chappell et al. (2008)
object: Chappell et al. (2008) noted that other reported cases had overlapping patterns, including malrotation, biliary atresia, and pancreatic hypoplasia (e.g., as described by Martinez-Frias), and proposed that these cases may be variations of the same syndrome.

subject: Chappell et al. (2008)
object: Because their patient was born to consanguineous parents, Chappell et al. (2008) concluded that the disorder is likely inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

subject: Chappell et al. (2008)
object: In their patient, Chappell et al. (2008) sequenced genes known to cause monogenic diabetes (KCNJ11, ABCC8, GCK, IPF1, HNF1-beta, NeuroD1, and TCF7L2) and the candidate gene HNF6, which is involved in hepatobiliary and pancreatic development. They found no mutations.

subject: Martinovici et al. (2010)
object: Martinovici et al. (2010) reported a newborn of consanguineous parents who had multiple congenital anomalies: intrauterine growth retardation, intestinal atresia, gallbladder aplasia, and diabetes mellitus. The authors made a diagnosis of Martinez-Frias syndrome. The infant also had neonatal hemochromatosis, and the authors suggested that neonatal hemochromatosis may be part of the Martinez-Frias syndrome.

subject: Martinovici et al. (2010)
object: Martinovici et al. (2010) described Martinez-Frias syndrome as a very rare autosomal recessive phenotype whose gene had not yet been identified. Their patient was born to consanguineous parents.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) described human infants with neonatal diabetes and small bowel obstruction due to bowel atresia. Pancreas size was somewhat reduced, but the patients were not deficient in exocrine pancreatic enzymes. Autopsies of 2 cases showed normal-appearing exocrine pancreata with clusters of chromogranin A-positive cells but no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. The syndrome also included a hypoplastic gallbladder and intractable diarrhea that did not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) mapped the disease locus by high-resolution homozygosity mapping in 2 probands, who were the offspring of first-cousin and second-cousin parents, respectively. Only 3 homozygous-by-descent regions were shared by both probands, totaling 24 Mb and containing 194 RefSeq genes. Of these genes, only RFX6, in the largest segment at 6q21-q22, showed pancreas-enriched expression, and its expression in fetal pancreas increased between 10 and 20 weeks.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) used array capture and deep sequencing of exons in the shared homozygous regions in proband 2. Of 30 novel sequence variants detected, the only nonsynonymous one was a ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in RFX6. Direct sequencing confirmed this variant in homozygous state in proband 2, the offspring of second cousins, who was alive at age 4.5 years. The variant was inherited from carrier parents. S217P lies between the DNA-binding and dimerization domains; it only modestly reduced DNA binding and did not affect dimer formation.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: In proband 1, the offspring of first cousins who died in the first few months of life, Smith et al. (2010) identified a homozygous loss of the RFX6 intron 2 splice donor site (IVS2+2T-C), inherited from carrier parents. RT-PCR of RNA from the proband's autopsy pancreas did not detect the properly spliced transcript. No RNA from exons 1 and 2 was detected either, which the authors attributed probably to nonsense-mediated decay.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) found a homozygous out-of-frame deletion in exon 7 of RFX6 in proband 4, who died in the first few months of life. The mutation was inherited from carrier parents.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) found a homozygous arg181-to-gln (R181Q) missense mutation in RFX6 in proband 5, who died in the first few months of life. The variant was inherited from carrier parents and affects a highly conserved arginine in the DNA-binding domain. In EMSA, R181Q completely abrogated DNA binding.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) found that proband 3 was compound heterozygous for 2 RFX6 splice mutations: a loss of the intron 6 donor site (IVS6+2T-G) and a disruption of the intron 1 acceptor site (IVS1-12A-G). Both mutations were inherited from carrier parents. This patient was still alive at age 9 years and was intermittently off insulin.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) found RFX6 mutations in 5 of 6 probands and described a genotype-phenotype correlation. Probands homozygous for a splice-site mutation, a frameshift deletion, or the DNA-binding-abolishing R181Q mutation died in the first few months of life. In contrast, the compound heterozygous proband 3 was alive at age 9 years, and proband 2, homozygous for the modestly hypomorphic S217P, was alive at age 4.5 years.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) described the human syndrome as autosomal recessive. The 2 mapped probands were the offspring of consanguineous parents (first and second cousins), and all identified RFX6 mutations were inherited from carrier parents.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) did not find an RFX6 mutation in proband 6. Because no DNA from the proband was available, they sequenced both parents and found no point mutation in RFX6 or NEUROG3; long-range PCR detected no RFX6 deletions. The authors considered this case most likely a phenocopy. They also found no RFX6 mutations in a case of Martinez-Frias syndrome.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) noted that OMIM had listed their cases under Martinez-Frias syndrome. They considered their cases distinct, because the original Martinez-Frias syndrome patients had esophageal atresia and hypospadias and did not have diabetes. They proposed the name Mitchell-Riley syndrome, after the 2 clinicians who first described the condition.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice by replacing the first 5 exons with an eGFP-cre cassette. Homozygous mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio but did not feed normally, had gross bowel distension due to small bowel obstruction, and died within 2 days of birth; some had reduced pancreas size. At embryonic day 17.5, the mutant pancreata contained many chromogranin A-positive endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin. Pancreatic polypeptide-expressing cells were increased.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: In Rfx6-null mouse pancreata, Smith et al. (2010) found that Neurog3 expression was unaffected. Expression of the alpha-cell factors Irx2 and Arx, and of the insulin transcription factors Pax6, MafA, NeuroD1, and Pdx1, was reduced. Nkx2.2 and Nkx6.1 were not significantly changed and Pax4 was increased, and Nkx6.1 expression expanded to all endocrine cells. Primary cilia formation was unaffected, in contrast to Rfx3-null mice.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) showed in mice that Rfx6 acts downstream of Neurog3. Rfx6 is expressed broadly in definitive endoderm after gastrulation, becomes restricted to the gut and pancreatic bud, is reactivated by Neurog3 in islet progenitor cells, and is finally restricted to the islets. The authors noted that NEUROG3 mutations also cause intractable diarrhea and diabetes but not small bowel atresia or biliary abnormalities. They attributed this difference to Rfx6 expression in early gut endoderm, where Neurog3 is not expressed.

subject: Smith et al. (2010)
object: Smith et al. (2010) showed by EMSA that Rfx6 and Rfx3 form a heterodimeric complex that binds an X box site. The 2 factors cooperated in activating a promoter containing multimers of this site. The authors concluded that Rfx3 and Rfx6 cooperate in regulating genes involved in islet development but not in cilia formation.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported a Turkish girl (case 1) born at 32 weeks' gestation (birth weight 1.65 kg) with duodenal atresia, jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum, who had hyperglycemia noted at age 2 years and presented at 3 years with diabetic ketoacidosis, very low insulin and C-peptide, and negative islet autoantibodies; she was treated with insulin. She had recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding due to gastric heterotopia in the small bowel, resolved after resection at age 5, and an absent gallbladder with normal liver function. Her identical twin had duodenal atresia and died at 1 month.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported the male double first cousin (case 2) of case 1, born at 34 weeks (birth weight 1.70 kg) with duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation, who had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia at age 5 and was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6 years with undetectable insulin, low C-peptide, and negative autoantibodies; he required insulin. He had chronic iron deficiency anemia of unknown cause and no hepatobiliary abnormality. The parents were not consanguineous, but the mothers were sisters and the fathers brothers.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: In 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes, Sansbury et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene, c.2176C>T (p.Arg726X) in exon 17 and c.2596C>T (p.Arg866X) in exon 18, by targeted next-generation sequencing confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The fathers were heterozygous for p.Arg726X and the mothers for p.Arg866X; both mutations were inherited from the grandmothers.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) found the RFX6 c.2596C>T (p.Arg866X) nonsense mutation in exon 18, in compound heterozygosity with p.Arg726X, in 2 double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome; it was inherited from the mothers. They predicted that p.Arg866X escapes nonsense-mediated decay because it lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary, producing a partially truncated protein with a preserved DNA-binding domain that might retain some function, whereas p.Arg726X is predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) noted that the 8 previously reported molecularly confirmed cases carried splicing/frameshift mutations in exons 2-8 or missense mutations within or near the DNA-binding domain and had diabetes onset within the first 2 weeks of life, whereas their patients carried the first truncating mutations at the 3-prime end (exons 17 and 18). They suggested that escape of the p.Arg866X allele from nonsense-mediated decay could allow retention of some RFX6 function, resulting in a milder phenotype with later onset of diabetes and absent liver pathology.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: In a review of 8 previously published molecularly confirmed Mitchell-Riley cases, Sansbury et al. (2015) found duodenal atresia in all, with or without jejunal atresia/midgut malrotation, gallbladder agenesis in 7 of 8, intrahepatic cholestasis in 7 of 8 and ascites in another, and death within the first year in 5 of 8. Their 2 new cases differed by childhood-onset diabetes and absence of liver pathology, with longer survival.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) found no evidence that heterozygosity for either RFX6 mutation in the family was associated with abnormal HbA1c or C-peptide levels or diabetes, although several heterozygous relatives had adult-onset diabetes; they noted it remained possible that carriers of 5-prime RFX6 mutations might have increased risk of early-onset type 2 diabetes.

subject: Sansbury et al. (2015)
object: Sansbury et al. (2015) recommended RFX6 genetic testing in infants with duodenal or jejunal atresia with or without intestinal malrotation even in the absence of neonatal diabetes, especially when sibling recurrence or parental consanguinity suggests autosomal recessive inheritance.
